title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course reviews the thoracic paravertebral block (TPVB), which has emerged as a safe and effective regional anesthetic technique for managing perioperative and postoperative pain. By providing unilateral, segmental somatic and sympathetic nerve blockade, TPVB reduces opioid consumption, minimizes the neuroendocrine stress response, and supports early rehabilitation. Its efficacy in thoracic, breast, and minimally invasive cardiac surgeries, particularly when guided by ultrasound to improve precision and safety, is also discussed.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Introduction
content: Lung cancer ranks among the leading causes of cancer-related mortality in both men and women and represents the second most commonly diagnosed cancer in the United States. According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), approximately 127,070 deaths from lung cancer are expected in 2023, accounting for roughly 20% of all cancer-related deaths. [1] Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comprises 84% of these cases, and thoracic surgery, including pulmonary lobectomy, remains the standard treatment. This surgical approach carries significant postoperative risks, including respiratory distress, bleeding, and pain, with pain contributing to pulmonary complications that occur in 40.8% of patients and delaying recovery, thereby impairing quality of life. [2]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Introduction
content: A meta-analysis of prospective studies reported chronic pain at 3 and 6 months in 57% of patients undergoing thoracotomy, reflecting the strong association between severe acute pain and the development of chronic pain. Regional anesthesia, particularly thoracic paravertebral block (TPVB), has demonstrated effectiveness in reducing postoperative opioid requirements and inflammatory response, ultimately improving postoperative outcomes and survival. [3] [4] First described by Hugo Sellheim in 1905 for abdominal analgesia, TPVB gained renewed attention in 1979 when Eason and Wyatt demonstrated the utility of catheter-based paravertebral nerve blocks and their beneficial effects. [5] Subsequent studies have consistently reported TPVB’s efficacy in reducing postoperative pain across various thoracic surgical procedures. [6] [7] [8]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Introduction
content: TPVB involves the injection of local anesthetic into the paravertebral space adjacent to the emerging spinal nerves at the intervertebral foramina. This technique achieves somatic and sympathetic nerve blockade across multiple thoracic dermatomes, providing effective regional analgesia for thoracic surgery. [9]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The triangle-shaped area between the head and neck of the rib. The paravertebral space is delineated anterolaterally by the parietal pleura, posteriorly by the costotransverse ligament, medially by the vertebrae and intervertebral foramina, and inferiorly and superiorly by the ribs. The vertebral root divides in this anatomical space after emerging from the intervertebral foramen to give the dorsal and ventral branches. Thus, the content of this space includes adipose tissue, anterior ramus of the spinal (intercostal) nerves, posterior ramus of the spinal (intercostal) nerves, sympathetic chain, and rami communicantes. The sympathetic chain communicates with the intercostal nerves via the rami communicantes. The thoracic paravertebral space communicates with the following: Medially: Epidural space via the intervertebral foramen [10] Laterally: Intercostal space [11] Superiorly: Cervical paravertebral space Inferiorly: The origins of the psoas major muscle

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The nerves in this space are devoid of the fascial sheath, making them particularly sensitive to local anesthetics injected. This injection of local anesthetic will cause unilateral, segmental, somatic, and sympathetic anesthesia, including the posterior branch in several thoracic dermatomes. [12] This extensive diffusion of the local anesthetic has been demonstrated by several authors, notably Cheema et al, using thermographic imaging. [9] Other authors have described diffusion of this nerve block into the epidural space, or even on the contralateral side of the block, as reported by Karmakar et al (2000) after injection of contrast medium through a thoracic paravertebral catheter. [13]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Indications
content: TPVB provides anesthesia and analgesia for surgical procedures involving a single hemithorax, particularly when pain is predominantly unilateral across the chest and abdomen. Perioperative use of bilateral TPVB has also been described during the thoracic phase of major abdominal surgeries. [14] TPVB often serves as an adjunct to multimodal postoperative analgesia in thoracic surgery, breast surgery, renal surgery, video-assisted thoracoscopic procedures, and minimally invasive cardiac surgery. Recent trends show increasing use of TPVB in breast reconstruction surgery in combination with general anesthesia to optimize pain control. [15] [16]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Indications
content: This nerve block offers an alternative anesthetic approach for breast surgery in patients at high risk for perioperative or postoperative complications following general anesthesia, including older adult patients with low vital capacity, limited pulmonary reserve, or underlying cardiac comorbidities. [17] [18] Multiple recent studies have demonstrated TPVB’s effectiveness in reducing postoperative complications and facilitating early rehabilitation, supporting its growing role in perioperative care. [19]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Contraindications
content: The main contraindications for TPVB include: Patient refusal Hypersensitivity reaction or allergy to local anesthetics Coagulopathy or systemic anticoagulation (INR >1.4 or insufficient time since stopping anticoagulant according to The American Society of Regional Anesthesia [ASRA] guidelines) Infection at the injection site Tumor occupying the region Respiratory infection, or persistent pleural enlargement, due to the risks of pneumothorax Deformity of the rib cage may predispose to a pleural or intrathecal puncture

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Equipment
content: The TPVB is currently performed in the majority of hospital institutions under ultrasound guidance to minimize the risk of nerve or pleural damage, which can lead to pneumothorax. To perform the procedure, the following equipment is necessary: Ultrasound guidance with the high-frequency probe or low-frequency curvilinear probe, depending on the patient's body Sterile sleeve and gel One 23- to 25-gauge needle for skin infiltration 25 mL of local anesthetic Needle size: 80mm B-bevel nerve block needle 1 pack of gauze 4-inch x 4-inch Chlorhexidine gluconate solution for skin asepsis Sterile gloves Marking pen for anatomical landmarks

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Personnel
content: Staff qualified in regional anesthesia are recommended for this procedure, as they must manage complications related to the nerve block. Before performing the procedure, administration of an anxiolytic may be necessary to reduce stress for some patients. Additionally, a nurse trained in regional anesthesia should accompany the physician during the procedure and assist with sedation if necessary.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Preparation
content: Before any regional anesthetic procedure, a complete checklist assessment should be performed. An assessment of the patient's comorbidities should be performed beforehand, including medical history, physical examination with evaluation of the respiratory tract, and analysis of preoperative tests. Before obtaining informed consent from the patient, the anesthesiologist must inform the patient of the risks and benefits of TPVB and the potential complications.

content: A clinic specializing in regional anesthesia is recommended to perform the nerve block to ensure optimal monitoring of patients' vital signs. This monitoring includes pulse oximetry, electrocardiography, and blood pressure, as described in the standards of the American Society of Anesthesiologists.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Technique or Treatment
content: Several techniques have been described for performing TPVB, with patient positioning in the seated, lateral, or prone position depending on comfort and procedural requirements. The sitting position often provides greater comfort for awake patients.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Technique or Treatment
content: The classical technique, widely used and described by Eason and Wyatt in 1979, relies on loss of resistance to identify the paravertebral space. [5] After aseptic preparation, the needle is inserted 2.5 to 3 cm lateral to the spinous process and advanced perpendicular to the skin until it contacts the transverse process of the lower vertebra. The needle is then carefully advanced over the transverse process until the anesthesiologist detects a loss of resistance to air, indicating passage through the costotransverse ligament. Following gentle aspiration, local anesthetic is injected into the paravertebral space.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Technique or Treatment
content: Due to a significant failure rate and risk of parietal pleura injury leading to pneumothorax, many centers have shifted toward ultrasound-guided TPVB. In 2009, Luyet et al demonstrated cadaveric catheter placement under ultrasound guidance, and subsequent studies have confirmed the technique’s accuracy and safety. [20] [21]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Technique or Treatment
content: After aseptic preparation extending from the cervicothoracic paravertebral region to the lower edge of the scapula, the anesthesiologist locates the paravertebral space from T2 to T6 at the surgical site using a 50 mm, 15-6 MHz linear ultrasound probe. [21] The spinous processes from T1 to T8 are identified either from the C1 vertebra or by referencing the scapula’s lower edge, corresponding to T7. Positioning the probe over the relevant spinous process, the examiner visualizes the transverse processes by lateral probe movement and identifies 3 key anatomical structures through an oblique probe angle: the double layer of the internal intercostal membrane, the transverse process, and respiratory movements of the parietal pleura. After skin anesthesia with 1 mL of 2% lidocaine, the needle is advanced out of plane, positioned 1 cm caudal to the probe, and inserted into the space between the internal intercostal membrane and pleura. Local anesthetic is then administered gradually over 30 seconds.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Complications
content: TPVB carries risks common to regional anesthesia, including puncture site infections, hematoma formation, nerve injury, and local anesthetic toxicity due to overdose. In addition, TPVB is associated with procedure-specific complications, eg, pneumothorax, hemothorax, and inadvertent intrathecal injection, as documented by Lekhak and colleagues. [22] Pulmonary hemorrhage has also been reported in patients undergoing paravertebral block during thoracic surgery. [23]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Complications
content: Other documented complications include ipsilateral brachial plexus block and hemidiaphragmatic paresis, as observed by Steven H. Renes et al. [24] Studies by Burlacu et al and Crawley S. M. described diffusion of local anesthetic to the ipsilateral stellate ganglion during TPVB, resulting in ipsilateral Horner syndrome. [25] [26] Advances in ultrasound technology and image-guided techniques have significantly reduced the incidence of these complications, improving the safety profile of TPVB in modern clinical practice.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Clinical Significance
content: TPVB is a regional anesthetic procedure associated with a low overall incidence of complications, thanks to ultrasound. It suppresses the neuroendocrine response to surgical stress by its somatic and sympathetic nerve blockade, allowing major thoracic surgery to be performed with optimal intraoperative and postoperative analgesia. The thoracic epidural is considered the gold standard for analgesia during a major thoracotomy, but TPVB, compared with the thoracic epidural, also provides effective pain relief with few adverse effects and should be considered a safe alternative in cases of contraindication to the thoracic epidural. [27]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Clinical Significance
content: In the current literature, multiple studies have demonstrated the impact of TPVB and its benefits for optimizing intraoperative and postoperative analgesia. These investigations include randomized controlled trials, observational trials, and numerous case reports. In a recent study including patients with NSCLC undergoing lobectomy surgery, ultrasound-guided TPVB demonstrated effectiveness in reducing postoperative pain, improving quality of life, and enhancing recovery for early revalidation. [15]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Clinical Significance
content: A single thoracic paravertebral injection is effective for acute pain control in the emergency room in patients with multiple posttraumatic rib fractures. To assess the analgesic efficacy of TPVB in patients scheduled for modified radical mastectomy, a prospective randomized trial was published recently, including 90 females. Postoperative morphine consumption during the first 48 hours was recorded. The study concluded that the TPVB allowed a significant reduction in postoperative opioid consumption compared to the control group, without an increase in adverse effects. [6]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Clinical Significance
content: Furthermore, in a recent meta-analysis, the analgesic efficacy of pectoral block was compared to TPVB at 2 postoperative hours in patients who had undergone breast surgery. After reviewing 8 trials involving 388 patients, the study concluded that, compared with paravertebral block, there is low-quality evidence that a pectoral block provides a marginal postoperative analgesic benefit after a radical mastectomy. [28] In another recent study, the authors evaluated retrospectively opioid consumption in patients who underwent video-assisted thoracic surgery after placing a paravertebral catheter. [29] A total of 269 patients were enrolled in this study, which concluded that TPVB appears to be a safe and effective analgesic technique for reducing postoperative pain and improving patient satisfaction.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Clinical Significance
content: In a prospective, randomized, controlled study, H Hu et al included 60 patients who underwent single-port video-assisted pulmonary lobectomy with a paravertebral block guided by thoracoscopy at the end of the operation. The visual analog score of the TPVB group was significantly lower than that of the control group at all time points. The author concludes that the regional analgesic procedure chosen for these patients can effectively reduce postoperative pain while ensuring patient safety. [30]

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: TPVB is a regional anesthetic technique used to provide effective anesthesia and analgesia for unilateral thoracic and abdominal surgical procedures. By targeting the paravertebral space near the emerging spinal nerves, TPVB achieves somatic and sympathetic nerve blockade across multiple thoracic dermatomes, reducing postoperative pain, opioid requirements, and inflammatory response. This technique has proven beneficial in thoracic surgery, breast surgery, minimally invasive cardiac procedures, and major abdominal operations, particularly in patients at high risk for complications under general anesthesia. Ultrasound guidance has enhanced the safety and accuracy of TPVB, minimizing complications such as pneumothorax, hemothorax, intrathecal injection, brachial plexus block, hemidiaphragmatic paresis, and Horner syndrome.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective implementation of TPVB requires advanced clinical skills, anatomical knowledge, and procedural expertise. Physicians and advanced practitioners must determine indications, plan anesthetic strategy, and perform precise ultrasound-guided needle placement. Nurses play a key role in perioperative monitoring, early detection of complications, and patient education. Pharmacists ensure safe dosing of local anesthetics and adjunct medications. Collaborative communication among anesthesiologists, surgeons, nursing staff, and allied health professionals facilitates individualized care, optimizes postoperative recovery, reduces complications, and enhances overall patient safety and team performance.

content: A qualified nursing team for the operating room is recommended when performing the TPVB, and the management of postoperative pain by the regional anesthesiologist.

title: Thoracic Paravertebral Block -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Monitoring
content: The TPVB should be performed in a university hospital center equipped with cardiovascular and respiratory monitoring equipment to ensure optimal monitoring of vital parameters and to predict and manage complications as safely as possible. Although the safety in performing nerve blocks has increased under ultrasound guidance, complications may still arise, and a qualified anesthesiologist should be well-equipped to manage them.
